title: The Emperor's Lightweight Crown (TA)
summary: Akbar complains of a headache from his jewel-encrusted crown. Birbal shows the Emperor that the weight of justice is the real burden of kingship. [TA]
full_text:
The imperial goldsmiths crafted a new ceremonial crown for Emperor Akbar, encrusted with rubies, diamonds, and emeralds set in solid gold. Wearing it for three hours during a state durbar, Akbar developed a severe headache.

Sitting in his private chamber, Akbar took off the crown, rubbed his temples, and complained to Birbal: 'This crown is magnificent, yet it is so terribly heavy! My neck aches, and my head throbs with pain! Have the goldsmiths hollow out the gold to make it light!'

Birbal picked up the glittering crown, held it in his hands, and said with gentle solemnity:

'Sire, the goldsmiths can remove half the gold and hollow out the frame, but the crown will remain just as heavy upon your brow.'

Akbar looked puzzled: 'How can it be heavy if the gold is removed?'

Birbal explained:

'Your Majesty, it is not the five pounds of gold and jewels that press down upon your forehead; it is the immense weight of the moral responsibility that the crown represents!

'When you place this crown upon your head, you carry the hopes, fears, tears, and justice of fifty million subjects across thirty provinces.

'You carry the burden of the starving peasant whose crops failed; the widow whose land was stolen; the soldier guarding the frozen northern borders; and the merchant sailing through storms.

'A tyrant wears a crown as a light toy of vanity, for he cares nothing for his people. But a just and noble monarch like Emperor Akbar feels the crushing weight of every decision, every law, and every life under his protection.

'No goldsmith on earth can lighten the crown of a righteous king, for justice is the heaviest burden given by heaven to man.'

Akbar sat in silent contemplation, his eyes moist with emotion. He placed the crown back upon his head with renewed resolve, thanking Birbal for reminding him of the sacred weight of royal duty.
